newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Diesel tankers line up at India Kandla port.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Diesel tankers line up at India Kandla port.

text.p: The closure of two floating jetties at the Indian west coast port of Kandla is expected to double tanker waiting time to more than 20 days, industry sources said on Friday.

Traders said they have been informed by Kandla port authorities that oil product tanker traffic, scheduled for discharge at the floating jetties, will be diverted to the three fixed jetties at the port.
"The waiting time for berthing at Kandla prior to the commissioning of the two jetties was around 20 days and this was reduced to five-six days," said a chemical trader.
"But now it will again be about 20 days," he said, referring to the loss of use of the two floating jetties.
The two floating jetties were commissioned in March and April but were closed down earlier this week after a collision involving two tankers.
Kandla is India's biggest oil port and handled about 8 million tonnes of petroleum products and 12.5 million tonnes of crude last year.
The closure is set to exacerbate a growing congestion problem at India's ports for petroleum products.
State-owned Indian Oil Corp has already cut back on diesel purchases this year because of congestion.

It purchased a massive 1.5 million tonnes for May imports, but by September purchases had fallen to 120,000 tonnes and in November the tender was cancelled. The IOC had already cancelled two kerosene tenders this year.

Tankers are also queuing at the east coast ports of Madras and Haldia with IOC purchases. Of the eight tankers waiting outside each port, three at Madras and six at Haldia are carrying diesel, shipping agents said.
The two floating jetties at Kandla are owned by Hindustan Petroleum Corp and IOC.
A Hindustan official said the company was evaluating the damage to its jetty and expected to know in about a week's time how long repair works would take.
He said he believed the other jetty suffered less damage and might be operational in one to two weeks. An IOC spokesman said he could not comment.
Shipping agents said state oil companies would seek approval for the port to give priority to handling diesel and other product so the 1,443 km Haldia-Batinda pipeline throughput would not suffer.
A shipping source said there were about 14 tankers waiting to discharge outside Kandla port, of which eight were carrying diesel.
In addition, there were 12 diesel tankers waiting outside the nearby Vadinar port for their cargoes to be loaded on to barges for eventual discharge at Kandla.
The IOC is expected to award its December diesel tender later on Friday, and traders said the IOC might try to keep purchases around at 300,000 to 350,000 tonnes.
Berth congestion was likely to be excercabated by IOC's move to begin liquified petroleum gas imports at Kandla from the end November, they said.
